Q1: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Maple St, chest pain, 7.8). It is the highest-scored waiting call: chest pain in a 68-year-old male outranks the twisted ankle (6.2) and the alarm activation (4.1). Q3: Dispatch the ladder truck to Call A (1st St, person trapped, 8.9). A trapped person on the 3rd floor with smoke showing edges out the elevator rescue (8.8), and the urgency score exists precisely to break this tie. Neither call hits 9.0, but holding the ladder would leave a trapped occupant waiting — highest urgency wins.
Q4: Dispatch the BLS unit to Call A (Hill Rd, diabetic emergency, 7.1). A real medical emergency scores well above the event standby (5.5), making Call A the clear priority. Units do not sit idle for a standby detail while a patient waits.
Q5: Dispatch the medic to Call A (River St, difficulty breathing, 8.1). The scores are nearly tied, but 8.1 beats 8.0, and difficulty breathing carries immediate airway risk that justifies the tiebreak to Call A. When scores are close the highest number still wins — never hold the unit waiting for something worse.
Q6: Dispatch the engine to Call A (Main St, vehicle fire, 6.8). It outscores the brush fire (6.5), and per the threshold protocol mutual aid is not required below 9.0 — the neighboring offer is a courtesy, not an escalation trigger. Holding the engine while two scored fires wait would be wrong; dispatch normally to the highest scorer.

Q8: Dispatch the medic to Call A (Cedar Ln, stroke symptoms, 8.7). Stroke is time-critical with a closing treatment window, and 8.7 is the highest score in the queue — well above the abdominal pain (7.3). Every minute held idle is brain lost; dispatch the highest scorer.

An idle engine with a scored call waiting is the failure the threshold section warns about: dispatch, do not hold.
